w: What's tested Feedback inhibition, and how to read primary versus secondary lab patterns (the gland's hormone against TSH) Anterior versus posterior pituitary; the five anterior cell types, their seven hormones, and the hypothalamic hormones that control them Pituitary adenomas (PitNETs): microadenoma versus macroadenoma, mass effect, bitemporal hemianopsia, and the functioning types Hypopituitarism: the 75 percent rule, Sheehan syndrome, null cell adenomas, empty sella, and the symptoms The posterior pituitary: ADH and oxytocin, central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and SIADH Thyroid development (lingual thyroid, thyroglossal duct), follicular versus C cells, and goiter Hyperthyroidism and Graves disease; hypothyroidism, myxedema, cretinism and Hashimoto thyroiditis Thyroid tumors: follicular adenoma and follicular, papillary, medullary and anaplastic carcinoma: how each looks under the microscope, its mutation, how it spreads and how it is treated Dr. Melad Dababneh, a pathologist at UAB and section head of head and neck pathology, gives this lecture, based on Dr. Bell's. Part 1 covers the pituitary and the thyroid; Part 2, the next hour, covers the parathyroid and adrenal glands. He told the class he mostly sees thyroid and parathyroid in his own practice, and he spent the most time on how to read thyroid labs and on the thyroid tumors. The endocrine system and feedback inhibition The endocrine system is an integrated group of organs whose job is to keep the body in metabolic balance: hormones, salt, sugar and energy. The organs in these two lectures are the pituitary, thyroid, parathyroids and adrenal glands. They make hormones, chemical messengers that act on receptors of target cells. Chemically, hormones are polypeptides, amines or steroids. Steroid hormones are fat-soluble, so they cross the cell membrane, which is mostly fat, and can move into the nucleus and bind DNA. Polypeptide and amine hormones interact only with receptors on the cell surface. Hormones are controlled by feedback inhibition: if you have a lot of a hormone, you shut it off; if you have too little, you make more. Dr. Dababneh's example is the thyroid axis. The hypothalamus releases thyrotropin-releasing hormone, or TRH, which tells the anterior pituitary to release thyroid-stimulating hormone, or TSH, which tells the thyroid to release T3 and T4. Once T3 and T4 reach the right level, they send a message back to the pituitary to stop sending TSH, and to the hypothalamus to stop sending TRH. If any link in this loop is injured, the hormone is over- or underproduced. For example, if the pituitary stops responding to feedback and keeps releasing TSH, the thyroid keeps making hormone and the patient becomes hyperthyroid. The same logic holds for every gland the pituitary talks to. The pituitary gland: two lobes The pituitary sits in the sella turcica, just above the sphenoid bone at the skull base, with the optic chiasm close above it. It has two lobes that are built differently. The anterior lobe, or adenohypophysis, "adeno" for gland, is made of secretory epithelial cells: a true gland. The posterior lobe, or neurohypophysis, is made of unmyelinated nerve fibers carrying neurosecretory granules of stored hormones. The fibers are axons from the hypothalamus, supported by modified glial cells called pituicytes. Anterior pituitary cells and their controls The anterior pituitary has five cell types that make seven hormones: two of the cell types make two hormones each. Dr. Dababneh's tip is that the name of the cell tells you what it makes; a gonadotroph, for example, serves the gonads. Somatotrophs Growth hormone (GH) GHRH releases; somatostatin inhibits Mammotrophs Prolactin TRH releases; dopamine inhibits Corticotrophs ACTH and MSH CRH releases Thyrotrophs TSH TRH releases Gonadotrophs FSH and LH GnRH releases Notice that TRH releases two hormones, TSH and prolactin, from two different cells. The two inhibitors are somatostatin, which stops growth hormone, and dopamine, which stops prolactin. Pituitary adenomas, now called PitNETs A benign neoplastic proliferation of the anterior pituitary is a pituitary adenoma, recently renamed a pituitary neuroendocrine tumor, or PitNET. The pituitary is a neuroendocrine organ and its cells stain with neuroendocrine markers, so the new name lines it up with neuroendocrine tumors elsewhere in the body. In everyday practice, pathologists still say pituitary adenoma. Adenomas are sorted two ways. By function: a functioning adenoma overproduces a hormone, and its symptoms depend on which one; a nonfunctioning adenoma makes no hormone and is just a mass. By size: A microadenoma is less than 10 millimeters. The slide says microadenomas make up half of all hyperfunctioning tumors; in class Dr. Dababneh put it the other way round, that most microadenomas are hyperfunctioning. Either way, the small ones usually come to attention through the hormone they make, and the large ones through their size. A macroadenoma is greater than 10 millimeters. These come with local mass effect, often before any hormone symptoms: enlargement of the sella turcica, increased intracranial pressure, whose main symptoms are nausea and vomiting, headache and double vision. Because the optic chiasm sits right above the sella, a macroadenoma pushing upward can press on the chiasm or the optic nerves. Pressure on the chiasm hits its crossing central fibers and spares the uncrossed lateral fibers, so the outer half of each eye's field is lost: bitemporal hemianopsia, starting in the upper temporal quadrants. Hyperpituitarism: the functioning adenomas Hyperpituitarism, excess hormone from the anterior pituitary, almost always means an adenoma. The rare causes are carcinoma, nontumorous hyperplasia, hypothalamic lesions and visceral cancers. The picture depends on which cell type has proliferated. Somatotroph tumors make growth hormone. They are the largest adenomas; their clinical signs are often subtle, and mass effects are frequent. Age decides the picture. In a child, excess growth hormone causes gigantism: the child grows bigger and taller. In an adult, it causes acromegaly: the internal organs and some bones enlarge, so the skull and head get bigger and the vertebrae enlarge. Because growth hormone interacts with glucose, many patients have glucose intolerance or diabetes, and the slide adds osteoporosis and hypertension. Prolactinomas, tumors of the mammotrophs, are the most common hyperfunctioning pituitary tumor. Prolactin helps control the menstrual cycle and milk release, so a prolactinoma causes the amenorrhea-galactorrhea syndrome in women: milk from the breasts, which is galactorrhea, and, through negative feedback, a shutdown of the cycle, which is amenorrhea. They are usually microadenomas in premenopausal women. Corticotroph adenomas make ACTH, which stimulates excess adrenal cortical steroids. They tend to be microadenomas, and they cause Cushing disease: obesity, especially central obesity, a moon face, hypertension and diabetes. Gonadotroph adenomas make FSH and LH but have no associated clinical syndrome; at most they may disturb the monthly cycle. They are usually macroadenomas, come to medical attention through local mass effect, and are then diagnosed by the elevated FSH and LH. They make up 10 to 20 percent of macroadenomas in middle-aged men and women. The gland has a large reserve: it appears only after about 75 percent of the anterior pituitary parenchyma is lost. Less commonly, a disorder of the hypothalamus, such as a hypothalamic tumor, stops the releasing factors from reaching the pituitary. The causes on the slide: Non-secretory, or "null cell," adenomas: the tumor makes no hormone, and as a mass it shuts down the normal gland. Ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary, classically Sheehan syndrome: around delivery, a sudden drop in blood pressure stops the pituitary's blood supply, and the gland shuts down abruptly. Ablation of the gland. Empty sella syndrome: an enlarged, empty sella turcica from chronic herniation of the subarachnoid space through a defect in the diaphragma sellae; the classic patients are obese, multiparous women. Dr. Dababneh said you don't need all of the details, only that the sella can turn up without its pituitary. Inflammatory lesions, trauma and metastatic neoplasms. The symptoms depend on which hormones are missing: fatigue, weight loss, decreased sex drive, sensitivity to cold, decreased appetite, facial puffiness, anemia and infertility. Women may have hot flashes, irregular or absent periods, loss of pubic hair and an inability to produce milk for breastfeeding. Men may have decreased facial or body hair. The posterior pituitary: ADH and oxytocin The posterior pituitary holds pituicytes and axons from two hypothalamic nuclei, the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei. Its two hormones, antidiuretic hormone, or ADH, and oxytocin, are made in the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary. Oxytocin potentiates uterine contractions and milk ejection. No clinical syndromes are associated with it. ADH maintains serum osmolality. It acts on the renal tubules to reabsorb water, and it also causes vasoconstriction. Its name is the hint: it works against diuresis. Diabetes insipidus and SIADH Dr. Dababneh's advice is to let ADH's name carry you. "Diabetes" just means polyuria, a lot of urine. Diabetes insipidus has nothing to do with sugar, unlike diabetes mellitus. It is a lack of ADH action: the tubules can't take water back, so it flushes out. Central diabetes insipidus is a deficiency of ADH. The patient has polyuria, a low urine specific gravity, and a high serum sodium and osmolality. The causes are head trauma, neoplasms, inflammatory disorders and surgery involving the pituitary or hypothalamus. In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, ADH is normal but the kidneys don't respond to it: resistance at the end organ. The syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion, or SIADH, is the opposite. ADH keeps being released without regard to serum osmolality, water is retained, body fluids are diluted, and the patient has hyponatremia, a low sodium. The most common cause is ectopic ADH production by a nonendocrine tumor, small cell carcinoma of the lung. A normal gland weighs about 25 grams. It develops from an evagination of pharyngeal epithelium at the back of the tongue that descends to its normal place in the neck. That downward migration explains its developmental anomalies, and they are ones a dentist can meet: Lingual thyroid: thyroid tissue left in the base, or posterior third, of the tongue. Thyroglossal duct cyst: the duct connecting the posterior tongue to the thyroid fails to go away. Substernal gland: thyroid tissue that has gone too far down, into the chest under the sternum. Ectopic thyroid tissue can sit anywhere along that midline path. Most thyroid cells are follicular cells, or thyrocytes, which make T3 and T4; these regulate carbohydrate, lipid and protein metabolism. The parafollicular cells, or C cells, sit beside the follicles and make calcitonin, which works on bone: it promotes the uptake of calcium into bone and inhibits bone resorption. Goiter Goiter is enlargement of the thyroid; in the classic picture, a diffuse enlargement of the whole gland rather than one lobe or one nodule. Endemic goiter comes from iodine deficiency, the most common cause. Sporadic goiter comes from hereditary enzyme defects or is idiopathic. Goiter is a clinical term: an enlarged gland can have too much function or too little. A multinodular goiter has many nodules back to back through the gland instead of a smooth enlargement, and it can be hyperfunctioning. Primary versus secondary: reading the labs This was the lecture's most practical point. Primary means the problem is in the organ that makes the hormone. Secondary means that organ is responding to a stimulus from somewhere else, here the pituitary. Primary hyperthyroidism: the thyroid overproduces T3 and T4 on its own, from a tumor or Graves disease, and the high hormone shuts off TSH by negative feedback. T4 high, TSH low. Secondary hyperthyroidism: the pituitary overproduces TSH, which drives the thyroid. T4 high, TSH high. Primary hypothyroidism: the thyroid itself fails, and the pituitary responds by raising TSH. T4 and T3 low, TSH high. Secondary hypothyroidism: the pituitary isn't making TSH. T4, T3 and TSH all low. Dr. Dababneh: "That's like a typical question in anything. T3, T4 high, TSH low, that's primary. Both high, that's secondary. And this applies to any other organ where there's communication with the pituitary gland." He used the same rule for Cushing in the next hour. A quick way to hold it: when the gland's hormone and TSH move in opposite directions, feedback is working and the gland is the cause, which is primary. When they move in the same direction, the pituitary is driving or failing, which is secondary. Primary hyperthyroidism High Low Thyroid Graves disease Secondary hyperthyroidism High High Pituitary TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma Primary hypothyroidism Low High Thyroid Hashimoto thyroiditis Secondary hypothyroidism Low Low Pituitary Sheehan syndrome Hyperthyroidism and Graves disease Hyperthyroidism is a hypermetabolic state caused by elevated free T3 and T4. Thyroid hormone controls metabolism and energy, so everything runs fast: weight loss, tachycardia and arrhythmias, diarrhea, weakness, tremor, nervousness, sweating and heat intolerance. Dr. Dababneh also listed hypertension. The causes are Graves disease, a diffuse hyperplasia of the thyroid; exogenous thyroid hormone, taking too much; a hyperfunctional multinodular goiter, which the slide calls Plummer syndrome; and a hyperfunctional adenoma. Less common causes are thyroiditis, TSH-secreting pituitary adenomas, the secondary cause, and struma ovarii. Graves disease is the most common cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism. It is autoimmune: an IgG autoantibody stimulates the TSH receptor, so the gland overproduces. The whole gland undergoes diffuse hyperplasia of its follicular cells, giving a goiter, and many patients have Graves ophthalmopathy. It is about 5 times more common in women. Hypothyroidism, myxedema and cretinism Hypothyroidism is the mirror image: instead of everything running fast, everything slows down. In primary hypothyroidism, T4 and T3 are low and TSH is high; in secondary hypothyroidism, all three are low. The adult picture is called myxedema: apathy and mental sluggishness, weight gain, cold intolerance, lethargy, coarsening of the facial features, enlargement of the tongue and puffy hands, with puffiness from fluid in the legs and around the hands. The enlarged tongue and coarse face are findings a dentist may notice first. Dr. Dababneh admitted he wasn't sure why the tongue enlarges, "but that's what happens." Cretinism is hypothyroidism in childhood, and, like gigantism, it shapes the whole of development: impaired mental development, short stature, a large head and a large tongue. Its causes are iodine deficiency, enzyme deficiency and agenesis of the thyroid. Hashimoto thyroiditis Hashimoto thyroiditis, properly called chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, is a chronic autoimmune thyroiditis and the most common cause of hypothyroidism in the US. In this lecture, its antibodies are anti-TSH receptor antibodies that block the action of TSH, unlike the Graves autoantibodies, which stimulate the receptor. Same target, opposite effect. Under the microscope, the name describes the slide: many small lymphocytes infiltrate the gland and shut down the follicles. Compared with normal thyroid, which has few lymphocytes, the follicular cells have larger, irregular nuclei and pinker cytoplasm. Function Hyperthyroidism (most common endogenous cause) Hypothyroidism (most common cause in the US) Antibody (as taught) IgG that stimulates the TSH receptor Anti-TSH receptor antibody that blocks TSH The gland Diffuse hyperplasia of the follicular cells; goiter Lymphocytes infiltrate; follicular cells with larger, irregular nuclei and pinker cytoplasm Labs Free T4 high, TSH low Free T4 low, TSH high Also Graves ophthalmopathy; women 5 to 1 Proper name: chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis Thyroid tumors: how a pathologist sorts them Thyroid neoplasms are named for the cell they come from. Follicular cells give follicular adenomas, which are benign, and follicular carcinomas, plus a special and more common type, papillary thyroid carcinoma. The C cells give medullary carcinoma. The tumors differ in behavior, in look and in the mutation behind them. Dr. Dababneh said the mutation part isn't on the slides, but it is how he works in real practice: BRAF-mutated tumors are papillary carcinomas. They invade lymphatic spaces and go to the lymph nodes. RAS-like tumors, with an NRAS or HRAS mutation, are follicular tumors. They stay confined and may invade their capsule or vessels; the carcinomas spread by angioinvasion, through blood vessels, to distant organs rather than to lymph nodes. RET mutations drive medullary carcinoma. Follicular adenoma The benign follicular tumor is encapsulated, normal-appearing thyroid tissue: well circumscribed, with an intact fibrous capsule all the way around, not invading anything. It is usually solitary, presents as a painless cold nodule, rarely hyperthyroid, and may cause difficulty swallowing. It can be functioning or nonfunctioning; a hyperfunctional adenoma is one of the causes of hyperthyroidism. Follicular carcinoma Follicular carcinoma is a malignant neoplasm with follicular differentiation: an encapsulated lesion with invasion through the capsule or into blood vessels. Invasion is what separates it from the adenoma. Capsular invasion looks like a mushroom: the tumor pushes up through the capsule and spreads out on top of it. In vascular invasion, tumor sits inside a vessel, a space lined by endothelial cells. It is more common in women, with a mean age at diagnosis of about 50. It is classified by how far it has invaded: Minimally invasive: grossly encapsulated, with capsular invasion only on histology. Encapsulated angioinvasive: grossly encapsulated, with vascular invasion on histology. Widely invasive: widespread infiltration of blood vessels, four or more on the slide (in class he said more than four), and of the adjacent thyroid tissue, sometimes beyond the gland. One slide shows a tumor invading through the thyroid cartilage into the larynx. Its metastases are blood-borne, most often from widely invasive tumors: to the lung and to bones, namely the shoulder girdle, sternum, skull and iliac bones. Dr. Dababneh's general rule for any tumor that spreads through blood vessels is to think of liver, lung, bone and brain. For follicular carcinoma, removing the lobe that holds the tumor, a hemithyroidectomy, is enough. Papillary thyroid carcinoma Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer, 60 to 80 percent of cases. It usually occurs under 40, is linked to radiation exposure rather than iodine deficiency, and grows slowly, with a 10-year survival greater than 80 percent. It spreads through lymphatics, and it can be solitary or multifocal. Dr. Dababneh: "It's important to know that they can be multifocal, because the treatment for PTC is different than the treatment of FTC." For follicular carcinoma a hemithyroidectomy is enough; for papillary carcinoma the entire thyroid is removed, because the other lobe might hold another focus. How it looks under the microscope: Papillary architecture: instead of follicles back to back, there are fronds built on a fibrovascular core, a small blood vessel in the middle, with the tumor cells lining it. The nuclei are the key. Compared with normal tissue or follicular tumors, they are enlarged and overcrowded, overlapping instead of respecting one another, with irregular membranes. Most importantly, they are hypochromatic, not hyperchromatic: pale and clear-looking, with the chromatin pushed to the edge. This look was named Orphan Annie eye nuclei. Nuclear grooves: where the irregular membrane dips inward, the dip, seen edge-on on a flat slide, looks like a line across the nucleus. Nuclear pseudoinclusions: when the dip deepens until the membrane meets itself, a lobule of cytoplasm is trapped inside the nucleus. A groove comes before an inclusion. Grooves and inclusions are features of the BRAF mutation that defines papillary carcinoma. Psammoma bodies, in about 50 percent of cases. Papillae float on a small capillary and can die out; when they die, they calcify in laminated layers. When a true psammoma body is seen in the thyroid, papillary carcinoma is presumed. Mutation RAS-like RAS BRAF What makes the diagnosis An intact capsule, no invasion Invasion of the capsule or vessels The nuclei, with papillary architecture Nuclei Normal-appearing Without the papillary nuclear changes Enlarged, overcrowded, pale (Orphan Annie eye), grooves, pseudoinclusions Psammoma bodies Not expected Not expected In about half Spread None Blood: lung and bone Lymphatics: neck nodes Focality and surgery Usually solitary Hemithyroidectomy is enough Can be multifocal: the whole gland is removed Who Solitary cold nodule Women, mean age about 50 Under 40, radiation exposure Medullary thyroid carcinoma Medullary carcinoma does not come from the follicular cells. It comes from the parafollicular C cells, which make calcitonin. It is usually infiltrative rather than well circumscribed. Sporadic, about 80 percent: a solitary lesion, mean age 45. Familial: younger patients, mean age 35; often multiple and bilateral; with associated C-cell hyperplasia; a component of MEN 2A and MEN 2B, through a germline RET mutation. Not RAS, not BRAF. Under the microscope it makes no thyroid hormone and no colloid. It looks like a neuroendocrine tumor: a solid, nested pattern of growth with a somewhat spindled quality. It also produces amyloid, which shows apple-green birefringence, and amyloid is a hint to the diagnosis. Immunohistochemistry confirms it: the tumor turns brown for calcitonin, its product, for chromogranin and synaptophysin, the neuroendocrine markers, and for CEA. In class, Dr. Dababneh added that because these tumors overproduce calcitonin, patients might have symptoms of hypercalcemia. That does not fit calcitonin's action on the slide, which moves calcium into bone and blocks bone resorption and so would lower blood calcium, not raise it. The two sources disagree, so this hub does not test calcium in medullary carcinoma; the safe facts are the C-cell origin, calcitonin as its product and marker, amyloid, and RET. Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma The tumors above are well differentiated: they still look and stain like thyroid. Anaplastic, or undifferentiated, carcinoma has lost its differentiation; taken out of the neck, you couldn't tell where it came from. It is about 10 percent of thyroid cancers, at ages 60 to 80, often in areas of endemic goiter. It is a rapidly fatal neck mass that grows within a couple of months, invades the thyroid cartilage, the skin and the surrounding skeletal muscle, and metastasizes. It carries many mutations, such as p53. The biopsy shows high-grade nuclei and a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, resembling no particular tissue, and it may not even stain for thyroid markers. Dr. Dababneh called it one of the emergencies in his job: tell the clinicians at once and send the tissue straight for molecular testing, hoping for a mutation they can target, such as BRAF, because most patients die without one.
